rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Nitric acid wears two hats. As a **strong monobasic acid** it neutralises bases and carbonates like any acid; as a **graded oxidising agent** it is unmatched. The concentration code rules everything: **concentrated acid stops at brown NO₂** (Cu + 4HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2NO₂), **dilute acid reaches colourless NO** (3Cu + 8HNO₃), and **very dilute acid with Zn, Mg or Mn drives nitrogen to N₂O or NH₄NO₃** — hydrogen is…

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "Nitric acid is both a strong acid and a strong oxidising agent; with metals it rarely, if ever, liberates hydrogen."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***The tanker paradox*** — concentrated nitric acid travels the country in aluminium tanks: the same acid that dissolves copper leaves aluminium untouched because passivity seals the surface.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Nitric Acid's Full Job Description Row 65 named the oxyacids and sketched the Ostwald process; this topic puts nitric acid through its full working day — as a strong acid, as an oxidising agent of graded strength, its action on Zn, Mg, Fe, Cu, S, C, SO₂ and H₂S, and the brown-ring test for the nitrate ion.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 As an acid - Strong monobasic acid: HNO₃ → H⁺ + NO₃⁻ (fully ionised); turns blue litmus red, neutralises bases and basic oxides, reacts with carbonates and metals below hydrogen in reactivity without any redox: - NaOH + HNO₃ → NaNO₃ + H₂O; Na₂CO₃ + 2HNO₃ → 2NaNO₃ + H₂O + CO₂.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Conc=NO2 (brown), dil=NO (browns at mouth), very dil+Zn=NH4NO3. Non-metals: S->H2SO4, C->CO2, P->H3PO4. Passivity trio: Fe, Al, Cr. Brown ring = [Fe(H2O)5NO]2+, fragile.

rows.text: **NEB-style (3m): Describe the brown-ring test for the nitrate ion, giving the chemistry of ring formation.** — Take the nitrate solution in a test tube and add an equal volume of **freshly prepared FeSO₄ solution**; mix. Hold the tube inclined and run **concentrated H₂SO₄** carefully down the wall so it forms a separate lower layer.…  ·  **NEB-style (2m): Write balanced equations for the action of (a) concentrated and (b) very dilute nitric acid on zinc, naming the nitrogen product in each.** — **(a) Concentrated:** **Zn + 4HNO₃(conc) → Zn(NO₃)₂ + 2NO₂ + 2H₂O** — nitrogen is reduced only to **NO₂**, seen as brown fumes.…

rows.text: In the brown-ring answer, the marker wants: fresh FeSO4, careful layering of conc H2SO4, the complex name/formula, and the warning not to shake — each scores.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: The deeper the dilution, the deeper the reduction: NO3- + H+ is the true oxidant, so concentrated acid stops at NO2 while very dilute acid with active metals drives nitrogen all the way to ammonium — always write the acid concentration over the arrow.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: HNO3 dual personality: strong monobasic acid (neutralises bases, carbonates) AND graded oxidant. Concentration code: conc -> NO2 (Cu + 4HNO3), dil -> NO (3Cu + 8HNO3), very dil + Zn/Mg/Mn -> NH4NO3 (4Zn + 10HNO3) or N2O with Mg (4Mg + 10HNO3).…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The brown-ring test has been a standard nitrate identification for over 150 years and still appears in NEB practical papers.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: **NEB-style (2m): What happens when concentrated HNO3 is heated with sulphur? Give the equation and identify the oxidation states.** — Sulphur is oxidised to sulphuric acid while the nitrate is reduced to brown NO₂: **S + 6HNO₃(conc) → H₂SO₄ + 6NO₂ + 2H₂O**.…

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ## 3. Scientific Definitions | Term | Scientific meaning | Example | |---|---|---| | **Monobasic acid** | One replaceable H per molecule | HNO₃ | | **Oxidising acid** | Acid whose anion is reduced while another species is oxidised | HNO₃ → NO₂/NO | | **Passivity** | Loss of expected reactivity due to a protective film | Fe in conc.…  ·  ## 4. Detailed Explanation ### 4.1 Why the reduction product deepens with dilution - The oxidising species is effectively NO₃⁻ + H⁺. Concentrated acid delivers a high oxidant flux, so the reduction stops early at NO₂ (a one-electron step).…  ·  ## 5. Comparison Tables | Feature | conc. HNO₃ | dil. HNO₃ | |---|---|---| | Reduction product | NO₂ (brown) | NO (colourless) | | With Cu | Cu(NO₃)₂ + NO₂ | Cu(NO₃)₂ + NO | | With Fe/Al | passive | dissolves (Fe³⁺/Al³⁺ + NO) | | Oxidising strength | highest | moderate | | Storage | Al tanks (passivity) | glass |

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Explain passivity with one industrial application.  ·  ## 6. Common Confusions - **"HNO₃ + active metal always gives H₂."** No — nitric acid is an oxidising acid; only very dilute acid with Mg/Mn gives traces of H₂ before oxidation takes over. Never write Zn + HNO₃ → Zn(NO₃)₂ + H₂ in an NEB answer.…  ·  ## 7. Exam Application - Quote equations with the acid concentration written over the arrow — markers look for (conc)/(dil) labels. - Brown-ring test: describe layering, name the complex, warn against shaking. - Passivity: name the metals (Fe, Al, Cr), the film (oxide), and the application (Al containers).
